summary: Psalm 98 begins by calling for a new song because Yahweh has acted in salvation and shown righteousness before the nations. The call widens from Israel to all the earth, then to the sea, rivers, and mountains. The psalm ends with creation singing because Yahweh comes to judge the world with righteousness and equity.
whyItMatters: This psalm connects God's faithfulness toward Israel with joy for the whole earth. In Book IV of Psalms, which emphasizes God's kingship, it presents righteous judgment as a reason for creation to sing.

context.author: Not named in the psalm; Psalms as a whole is an anthology with many writers and collections.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, later received by Jewish and Christian communities for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Psalm 98 does not identify a date or name a specific saving event. It belongs to an anthology assembled from poems of different periods.
context.setting: Book IV of Psalms, a section that emphasizes Yahweh's reign, creation, and enduring mercy after the crisis of the human throne.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, here a praise psalm that summons human worship and creation's response.

outline.heading: A New Song for Salvation
outline.note: The psalm begins with praise because Yahweh has done marvelous things, made salvation known, remembered Israel, and shown that salvation to the ends of the earth.

outline.heading: All the Earth Joins the Music
outline.note: The command to praise expands to all the earth, with singing, harp, trumpets, and the ram's horn before Yahweh the King.

outline.heading: Creation Sings Before the Judge
outline.note: Sea, world, rivers, and mountains are summoned into praise because Yahweh comes to judge the earth with righteousness and equity.

keyVerses.text: A Psalm. Sing to Yahweh a new song, for he has done marvelous things! His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the reason for the whole psalm: praise answers Yahweh's saving action.

keyVerses.text: He has remembered his loving kindness and his faithfulness toward the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.
keyVerses.why: The verse holds together Israel's particular memory and the psalm's worldwide horizon.

keyVerses.text: With trumpets and sound of the ram’s horn, make a joyful noise before the King, Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: This line names Yahweh as King and places the praise in public, musical language.

keyVerses.text: Let them sing before Yahweh, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity.
keyVerses.why: The ending explains why creation sings: Yahweh's coming judgment is described as righteous and equitable.

questions.question: Why does the call to praise expand to all creation?
questions.answer: The psalm calls for praise because Yahweh has acted in salvation. Verses 1-3 describe God's saving action for Israel as known throughout the earth. Verses 4-6 call the earth to sing with instruments, and verses 7-9 add the sea, rivers, and mountains. The widening chorus celebrates his righteous judgment.

questions.question: What does “new song” mean here?
questions.answer: The psalm does not define the phrase as a technical category. In this chapter, the new song is connected directly to Yahweh having done marvelous things and worked salvation. The focus is not novelty for its own sake, but a fresh act of praise answering what God has done.

questions.question: Who has seen Yahweh's salvation?
questions.answer: Verse 3 says, “All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.” The psalm first says Yahweh remembered loving kindness and faithfulness toward the house of Israel, then immediately says the sight of salvation reaches the ends of the earth. The chapter therefore moves from Israel's experience to worldwide witness.

questions.question: Why are musical instruments mentioned?
questions.answer: Verses 5-6 call for praise with the harp, trumpets, and the ram's horn. The psalm presents praise as voiced, public, and musical, though it does not give enough information to reconstruct one exact ancient performance. The instruments serve the larger summons to make a joyful noise before Yahweh the King.

questions.question: Why does the psalm call Yahweh “the King”?
questions.answer: Verse 6 says the joyful noise is made before “the King, Yahweh.” In this chapter, that kingship is shown through salvation, righteousness, and judgment. The psalm does not describe a human king; its focus is Yahweh's rule over Israel, the nations, and the world.

questions.question: Are the sea, rivers, and mountains literally praising?
questions.answer: The psalm personifies creation: rivers are given hands to clap, and mountains voices to sing. The sea's roar joins that imagined chorus. These images extend the call to praise beyond human worshipers, picturing the whole created world celebrating Yahweh's just rule.

questions.question: Is judgment supposed to be frightening or good news here?
questions.answer: The psalm presents Yahweh's coming judgment as a reason for singing. Verse 9 says he will judge with righteousness and equity, so the emphasis falls on right and fair rule. Creation's song presents that judgment as hope for the world and the peoples; the psalm does not describe particular sentences or penalties.

questions.question: Does this psalm speak only about Israel?
questions.answer: No. Israel is specifically named in verse 3 as “the house of Israel,” and Yahweh's loving kindness and faithfulness toward Israel are remembered. But the same verse says all the ends of the earth have seen God's salvation, and the following verses call all the earth and then creation itself into praise.

questions.question: How should a first-time reader follow the poem's movement?
questions.answer: Watch the widening circle. Verses 1-3 give the reason for praise, verses 4-6 command the earth to praise with music, and verses 7-9 summon creation to sing before Yahweh's righteous judgment. The chapter is short, but its scope moves from remembered salvation to the whole world before God.

glossary.def: The divine name used throughout this translation of the psalm for Israel's God.
A fresh song of praise in response to the marvelous things Yahweh has done.
The psalm's term for Yahweh's committed goodness remembered toward the house of Israel.
An instrument named with trumpets in the call to make a joyful noise before Yahweh the King.
Fairness or even-handed justice; in verse 9 it describes how Yahweh judges the peoples.
